correctness.rationale: For each prime power and all nonzero slopes the full \(3q-2\) dimensional input decomposes as one four-dimensional constant block and one three-dimensional block for each nontrivial multiplicative character. The constant block is proved injective, including isotropic directions. The nontrivial blocks have nonzero Gauss factors of modulus \(\sqrt q\) and two-by-two identity leading minors; each contributes one kernel vector exactly when its explicit character determinant vanishes. The unit-circle identity y=1+x forces conjugate sixth-root pairs, counted as \(2(q-1)/|\langle t^2,1+t^2\rangle|\), while \(t^2=-1\) yields \((q-1)/2\) in odd characteristic and zero in characteristic two. A polynomial-field program passed all 232 independently calculated matrix-rank comparisons. No step infers infinite claims from finite testing.

originality.rationale: The claim concerns a (\(3q-2\))-square nonorthogonal principal Fourier matrix and exact character-resonance nullities. Two full 2015 finite-field papers address orthogonal spectral pairs, tiling, cone Fourier zero sets and related finite-field methods but do not give the stated general rank classification; their conditions do not imply mere invertibility. A complete 2024 paper classifies only small principal minors in cyclic groups, not growing three-line submatrices of \(\mathbb F_q^2\). Closest indexed mathematical records concern only three-by-three affine-plane Fourier minors and previously studied two-line or graph-axis special geometries; those statements do not logically dominate the theorem. Originality remains bounded: equivalent older studies of three-line Fourier interpolation or Gauss-character block matrices could have been missed.

value.rationale: The union of three projective directions is the first nontrivial three-arm Fourier interpolation geometry. The result decides exact recoverability and lost dimensions over every finite field, separates characteristic-two rigidity from odd-characteristic isotropic and sixth-root obstructions, and supplies a concrete subgroup-index computation with distinct nullities even at fixed field order. It is not a low-order table computation or a reparametrization of the prior two-line and cycle-axis cases. The precise invariant, principal Fourier rank, is a natural criterion for an exponential sampling basis; nonorthogonal bases are meaningful even when orthogonal spectrality fails.
